system_map.overview: CAS is a CLI-driven continuous architecture system that orchestrates LLM-backed agents, enforces governance rules, and persists architectural knowledge in a git-based store. The system uses a central FlowRunner to execute deterministic step pipelines, with LLM access abstracted behind a provider-agnostic client and governance rules merged into agent configurations.

agents.name: FlowRunner
agents.role: Central orchestrator executing the governance/LLM pipeline step-by-step

agents.name: VerifierAgent
agents.role: Checks agent outputs for compliance and correctness before acceptance

agents.name: SkillExecutor
agents.role: Runs declarative agent skills (add-modify-feature, refactor-module, etc.)

orchestration.description: FlowRunner owns the execution sequence and passes a mutable context through a series of steps. Individual agents/skills execute autonomously within the boundaries of their definitions, but the overall flow is centrally controlled.

patterns.name: Orchestrated Runner Pipeline with Shared Context

tool_protocols.notes: LLM tool calls via LiteLLM, orchestrated by FlowRunner

optimisation_targets.notes: Deterministic step sequencing prioritises reproducibility over raw speed

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Central control with explicit step boundaries balances autonomy and predictability

patterns.summary: A central FlowRunner executes a deterministic sequence of steps, passing a mutable context object between each phase to propagate intermediate results.
patterns.intent: Execute multi-phase agentic workflows without hardcoding control flow per use case, while preserving the ability to trace how state evolves.
patterns.context: CAS CLI uses FlowRunner to coordinate LLM calls, compliance checks, and documentation generation. The runner is the single entry point for governance workflows.
forces: Need deterministic ordering of steps
Want to reuse steps across different workflows
Must pass intermediate results (LLM responses, compliance findings) to later steps
Need to keep orchestration logic separate from step internals
patterns.solution: FlowRunner maintains a step registry and iterates over it, updating a shared context dict after each step. Steps expose a prepare_inputs contract that reads from context and returns validated results, which are written back for the next step.
implementation_signals: Runner mutates a context object across steps
Step registry or list in runner

evidence.note: CLI entry point that triggers FlowRunner

benefits: Easy to add or reorder steps
Shared context allows cross-step state accumulation
costs: Sequential execution can bottleneck on slow LLM calls
Context object can become a dumping ground if not carefully contracted
failure_modes: Step ordering changes break implicit dependencies
Context mutation makes rollback difficult

patterns.reuse_notes: Applicable to any multi-step CLI or agent loop where a clear sequence of phases is needed; avoid if steps have complex parallelism or long-running async workflows.

patterns.name: LLM Provider Abstraction for Portability

tool_protocols.notes: LiteLLM client likely exposes tool-calling capabilities

optimisation_targets.notes: Mock client enables zero-cost testing; LiteLLM allows provider switching for quality/cost trade-offs

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Thin abstraction keeps agent logic independent of model specifics

patterns.summary: LLM calls are routed through a thin client interface with a mock implementation, decoupling agent logic from any specific model provider.
patterns.intent: Allow the system to run deterministically in CI without live API calls and to switch providers without rewriting agent logic.
patterns.context: src/cas_runner/llm/ contains LiteLLMClient (real) and MockLLMClient (test/dry-run). Dependencies include litellm and pydantic, indicating a typed interface.
forces: Testing governance logic in CI without incurring LLM costs
Need to support multiple model providers
Want to keep agent prompts and tool calls agnostic to provider-specific quirks
patterns.solution: Both clients implement the same call contract, likely with a common `complete()` or `generate()` method. FlowRunner selects the concrete client based on environment variables or CLI flags.
implementation_signals: Presence of both LiteLLMClient and MockLLMClient in same directory
pyproject.toml lists litellm as a dependency

benefits: Provider changes do not affect agent logic
costs: Abstraction layer may hide provider-specific capabilities
Additional abstraction can complicate debugging model behaviour
failure_modes: If mock client diverges from real client behaviour, tests may give false confidence
Provider-specific prompts or tools might not be portable

patterns.reuse_notes: Use a client interface with at least one mock implementation for any LLM-backed tool that needs CI testing or cost control.

patterns.name: Governance-as-Code Merger

tool_protocols.notes: No evidence of MCP or tool calling; merger is a pure file/config transformation

optimisation_targets.notes: Ensures consistent governance across agent configs without manual copies

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Central rules with agent-specific overrides maintains controlled autonomy

patterns.summary: Explicit governance rules are merged into each agent's configuration at onboarding time, ensuring all agents inherit project-wide constraints.
patterns.intent: Centralise architectural rules while allowing per-agent customisation, avoiding drift from manual copying.
patterns.context: AgenticMerger in src/cas_runner/governance/ merges a governance block into agent definition files. bootstrap.py applies this during workspace setup, alongside merge_claude_settings.
forces: Governance rules must be consistent across a repo
Agent-specific overrides are needed for special cases
Manual copy/paste causes drift and inconsistency
Onboarding should be repeatable and fast
patterns.solution: A canonical governance block (in AGENTS.md or a dedicated file) is parsed by AgenticMerger and merged into each agent config, preserving agent-specific settings while overlaying global rules. Bootstrap applies the merge during workspace initialisation.

benefits: Single source of truth for governance
costs: Merge conflicts or unexpected overrides
Need to version governance files carefully
failure_modes: Agent-specific config can override global rules unintentionally
Merge logic may not handle all edge cases (arrays, nested objects)

patterns.reuse_notes: Adopt for any system where multiple agents share common constraints but need individual customisation; ensure merge semantics are well-documented and tested.

patterns.name: Evidence-Driven Knowledge Memory

tool_protocols.notes: Knowledge store acts as a static blackboard; no MCP or tool calling directly evidenced

optimisation_targets.notes: Persisting decisions and patterns improves long-term consistency

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Agents write to shared knowledge but follow predefined schema and governance

patterns.summary: Architectural knowledge is persisted in a structured, git-versioned store (decisions, patterns, rules, signals) that serves as shared memory for agents.
patterns.intent: Maintain a long-term, evidence-first record of architectural decisions that agents can query and update without relying on ephemeral model context.
patterns.context: cas-knowledge/global/ contains subdirectories for decisions, governance, maps, models, narratives, patterns, rules, signals. Templates in cas-knowledge/templates/ enforce structure.
forces: Agents need consistent historical context
Decisions should be traceable to concrete artefacts
Knowledge must be versioned and reviewable
Avoid relying solely on LLM context windows
patterns.solution: A structured directory layout with markdown templates ensures that decisions, patterns, rules, and signals are recorded in a canonical format. Git provides versioning and review workflow; runtime traces provide execution evidence.

costs: Requires discipline to maintain structure
Knowledge can become stale if not updated
failure_modes: Files may become inconsistent without enforced schema
Agents may not query the store unless orchestrated to do so

patterns.reuse_notes: For multi-agent systems needing durable memory, adopt a versioned knowledge store with template-forced structure. Add tooling to query and update the store.

patterns.name: Declarative Skill Packages

tool_protocols.notes: Skills likely define tool-use protocols and are orchestrated by agents/subagents

optimisation_targets.notes: Standardised skills allow reuse of proven workflows

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Skills constrain agent actions to well-defined procedures, limiting uncontrolled behaviour

patterns.summary: Agent capabilities are encapsulated in declarative, reusable skill directories (SKILL.md + supporting scripts) that can be invoked across different agent frameworks.
patterns.intent: Provide a standardised way to package and invoke agent actions (e.g., add feature, refactor module) without embedding logic in prompts.
patterns.context: Repository defines multiple skills under .agents/skills and .claude/skills, including cas-add-or-modify-feature, cas-drawio-generator, cas-refactor-module, etc.
forces: Agent actions are repeated frequently
Need to share capabilities between Claude Code and other agent frameworks
Skills should be verifiable and versioned
patterns.solution: Each skill is a directory with a SKILL.md description and supporting files. The same skill directory is duplicated to both .agents and .claude to be available to both toolchains (with potential symlinking).
implementation_signals: Skills directories with dashes in names

benefits: Proven procedures are codified and versioned
Skills can be evaluated and improved
costs: Skill duplication across frameworks can cause drift
Skills need careful documentation to remain useful
failure_modes: Skill definitions can diverge between .agents and .claude
Skills may become stale as repository structure evolves

patterns.reuse_notes: Use a skill directory structure with SKILL.md and scripts. Consider symlinking to avoid duplication, and add evaluation harnesses for skills.

patterns.name: Verifier Guardrail Agent

tool_protocols.notes: Verifier likely uses tools/checks to validate outputs

optimisation_targets.notes: Dedicated verifier agent reduces risk of unchecked changes

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Autonomy is constrained by a separate verification step

patterns.summary: A dedicated verifier agent reviews agent outputs against governance rules and project context before changes are accepted.
patterns.intent: Prevent non-compliant or low-quality agent output from being merged without review.
patterns.context: Both Claude Code (via .claude/agents/verifier.md) and the broader agent system (via .agents/subagents/verifier.md) include a verifier subagent. This is complemented by compliance checks in src/cas_runner/governance/.
forces: Agents may produce plausible but incorrect changes
Governance rules must be enforced consistently
Human review every change is impractical; automated verification helps
patterns.solution: A verifier agent is defined with explicit instructions/rules to check proposed changes against governance rules and project standards. It runs after main agent output and before final acceptance, producing a pass/fail verdict.
implementation_signals: ComplianceEngine and compliance checks in src/cas_runner/governance/

evidence.note: Verifier agent config for agents framework

benefits: Provides an audit trail of verification
costs: Adds an extra processing step
Verifier may be bypassed if not integrated into workflow
failure_modes: Verifier becomes a rubber stamp if overly permissive
Verifier may duplicate checks already performed by main agent

patterns.reuse_notes: Incorporate a verifier agent or pass in any multi-agent pipeline where autonomous changes risk harming the repository. Ensure verifier has access to the same governance rules as the main agent.

patterns.name: Typed Contract Models for Agent Exchanges

tool_protocols.notes: Typed models serve as data contracts, not tool protocols

optimisation_targets.notes: Pydantic models ensure well-formed data between components and agents

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Strict schema limits flexibility but increases predictability

patterns.summary: Agent inputs/outputs and governance data are defined as pydantic models, providing runtime validation and a stable contract between components.
patterns.intent: Guarantee that agent-generated data conforms to expected structure, reducing silent failures and enabling tooling.
patterns.context: governance/models.py defines many models such as ResolutionResult, TraceableMetric, GovernanceHealth, ComplianceFinding. skills/models.py defines SkillEvalCase, SkillEvalSuite, etc.
forces: Agents/LLMs may produce unstructured or malformed data
Need to share data between steps and components reliably
Want to catch contract violations early
patterns.solution: All data crossing component boundaries is defined as pydantic models with validation. Models are used in governance and skill evaluation contexts, and likely also in step contracts.

costs: Over-strict schemas can reject valid variations
Model changes require updating all producers/consumers
failure_modes: If schema evolves, stale serialised data may fail validation
Models may become over-structured, reducing flexibility

patterns.reuse_notes: Use idiomatic typed models (pydantic/dataclasses) for any agent-generated structured output. Keep schema versioned to support migration.

patterns.name: Skill Evaluation Suite

tool_protocols.notes: Evaluations likely use LLM or scripted checks to assess skill output

optimisation_targets.notes: Systematic evaluation tracks skill improvements and regressions

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Evaluation is deterministic and outside agent autonomy

patterns.summary: Skills are accompanied by a formal evaluation suite defined by pydantic models, enabling automated scoring and regression detection.
patterns.intent: Ensure that agent skills remain effective over time by providing a reproducible evaluation framework.
patterns.context: src/cas_runner/skills/models.py defines SkillAssertions, SkillEvalCase, SkillEvalSuite, SkillEvalResult, SkillEvalReport with an EvalStatus enum.
forces: Skills evolve and may regress
Need objective measures of skill success
Want to compare different approaches
patterns.solution: Each skill can have test cases defined as SkillEvalCase with assertions. A runner executes the skill on each case, records results, and produces an aggregate report (SkillEvalReport).

evidence.note: CI workflow for running skill evaluations

costs: Writing good assertions is non-trivial
Evaluation runs may be slow or costly
failure_modes: Tests may be too narrow, missing real-world drift
Evaluation suite may not be updated when skills change

patterns.reuse_notes: For any reusable agent skill or prompt, define a small evaluation suite with typed test cases. Integrate into CI for continuous quality monitoring.

patterns.name: Workflow Validation Gates

tool_protocols.notes: Validation scripts operate on files, not via tool calling

optimisation_targets.notes: Automated checks enforce constraints without manual review

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Deterministic validation constrains agent-driven workflow changes

patterns.summary: CI workflows are accompanied by deterministic validation scripts that gate on hardcoded values, unpinned installers, and other risky patterns.
patterns.intent: Prevent unintended or non-compliant changes to CI workflows and infrastructure.
patterns.context: A spec-driven validation script (validate_workflows.py) checks for YAML syntax, zero hardcoding, no unpinned installers, no unreachable dry-run, retired workflow checks, and composite action adoption.
forces: CI workflows evolve over time and can regress
Need to enforce best practices without reviewing every PR manually
Validation must be fast and deterministic
patterns.solution: A dedicated validation script is run in CI (or locally) to enforce a list of rules, each implemented as a function (check_yaml_syntax, check_zero_hardcoding, etc.). Failures block the workflow.

evidence.note: Deterministic rules for CI workflow health

costs: Rules may be too strict, blocking legitimate changes
Validation adds one more thing to maintain
failure_modes: If rules are not updated, new anti-patterns may slip through
Rules may be bypassed by modifying the validation script itself

patterns.reuse_notes: Apply to any CI setup where workflows are agent-editable; encode a set of deterministic checks that are versioned and enforced before merge.

patterns.name: Configuration Synchronisation Across Agent Frameworks

tool_protocols.notes: Configuration sync is file-level, not tool-based

optimisation_targets.notes: Ensures consistent agent settings across tools without manual duplication

patterns.summary: Bootstrap script merges and synchronises agent configuration across different tools (e.g., Claude Code settings, AGENTS.md) and creates symlinks/copies to avoid drift.
patterns.intent: Provide a single onboarding entry point that ensures all agent tools have consistent governance and settings.
patterns.context: bootstrap.py includes merge_claude_settings, merge_cas_governance_block, and _create_symlink_or_copy, indicating that it synchronises .claude settings and governance block across files.
forces: Different agent frameworks read different config files
Manual sync causes drift
Onboarding should be repeatable and quick
patterns.solution: The bootstrap process reads canonical governance and settings, then writes or symlinks to the expected locations for each agent framework (e.g., .claude/settings.json). Symlinks avoid duplication, copies allow per-project overrides.

benefits: Single command to initialise a project
costs: Bootstrap may overwrite user customisations if not careful
Symlinks can break in some environments
failure_modes: Incorrect merge order can clobber user settings
Symlinks may not work on all operating systems

patterns.reuse_notes: Adopt a bootstrap script for any multi-agent toolchain that requires config in multiple places; prefer symlinks for canonical files and copies for overrides.

patterns.name: Execution Trace Logging

tool_protocols.notes: Trace logging is file and OTel based, not tool protocol

optimisation_targets.notes: Traces enable debugging and audit of agentic runs

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Logging is a passive, deterministic mechanism

patterns.summary: Every run records execution traces and profile data into a runtime directory, providing an audit trail for multi-step agent executions.
patterns.intent: Capture execution steps and outcomes for post-hoc analysis, debugging, and continuous improvement of agent workflows.
patterns.context: cas-knowledge/runtime/ contains traces/ and evaluations/, plus execution-profile.yaml. pyproject.toml includes opentelemetry, suggesting additional structured tracing.
forces: Agent executions may be non-deterministic
Need to understand why a particular decision was made
Want to evaluate and improve workflows over time
patterns.solution: FlowRunner and related services write trace files to cas-knowledge/runtime/traces/, recording step names, inputs/outputs, and timing. OTel integration adds standardised metrics.

benefits: Can be used for performance tuning
costs: Storage overhead for traces
Trace files may contain sensitive data if not sanitised
failure_modes: Traces may not include enough context without explicit instrumentation
Trace format may change and break analysis tools

patterns.reuse_notes: Instrument your orchestrator to record step-level traces to a dedicated directory; use a standard format for easy querying. Keep traces out of version control if sensitive.

patterns.name: Heuristic-to-Pattern Promotion

tool_protocols.notes: This is a knowledge management process, not a runtime execution pattern

optimisation_targets.notes: Promote proven heuristics into formal patterns for reuse

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Documented process for advancing knowledge while retaining flexibility

patterns.summary: The system provides a defined path for evolving ad-hoc heuristics into formal, reusable architecture patterns via templates.
patterns.intent: Capture emerging best practices and codify them into the knowledge base to improve future guidance.
patterns.context: cas-knowledge/templates/ contains heuristic-to-pattern_template.md and pattern_template.md, suggesting a structured process for converting heuristics into patterns.
forces: New insights arise from repeated practice
Without a process, heuristics remain informal and fade
Patterns should be validated and documented
patterns.solution: A template for heuristic-to-pattern promotion provides a structured way to document a heuristic, its evidence, and convert it to a pattern with consequences and reuse notes.

costs: Requires maintenance of knowledge base
Promotion process can be bureaucratic
failure_modes: Heuristics may be promoted without enough evidence
Pattern catalogue may become stale if not pruned

patterns.reuse_notes: Establish a lightweight promotion workflow from heuristics to patterns with templates, evidence requirements, and review checkpoints.

anti_patterns.name: Duplicated Agent Skill Definitions Across Frameworks
symptoms: Same skill name appears in .agents/skills and .claude/skills
Changes to one copy may not be reflected in the other
Skill eval may use one source while runtime uses another

where_observed.note: Skill defined for one agent framework
Same skill duplicated for another framework

impact: Skill versions drift, leading to inconsistent agent behaviour
Testing may target the wrong copy, giving false confidence
suggested_remediation: Use symlinks or shared submodules for skills
Add a CI check that verifies copies are identical
Define skills once and reference them via a canonical location

cross_cutting_concerns.approach: Pydantic models in governance/models.py and skills/models.py define structured contracts for agent inputs and outputs; templates enforce structure in the knowledge store.
cross_cutting_concerns.notes: Typed contracts reduce ambiguity and enable validation across components.

cross_cutting_concerns.approach: Skill evaluation models (SkillEvalSuite) and CI workflow cas-skill-evals.yml ensure skills are tested; compliance findings are recorded in governance models.
cross_cutting_concerns.notes: Evaluation is both deterministic (CI checks) and agent-driven (skill execution).

cross_cutting_concerns.approach: Verifier agent and ComplianceEngine enforce governance before merge; workflow validation gates catch disallowed CI patterns.
cross_cutting_concerns.notes: Safety is layered: automation, verification, and deterministic checks.

cross_cutting_concerns.approach: LiteLLM provider abstraction with MockLLM enables offline testing and cost-free evaluation; provider switching allows cost/quality trade-offs.
cross_cutting_concerns.notes: Abstraction reduces risk of vendor lock-in and supports controlled spending.

cross_cutting_concerns.approach: Execution traces stored in cas-knowledge/runtime/traces and OpenTelemetry dependencies provide insight into agentic runs.
cross_cutting_concerns.notes: Trace data enables post-hoc analysis and debugging of multi-step flows.
